newsitem.title: CANADA: FORECAST-Canada's economy to lead G7, poll says.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Canada's economy to lead G7, poll says.

text.p: Low inflation, stable interest rates and a growing trade surplus will push Canada's growth rate past all other G7 countries in the next two years, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
The quarterly survey, which polled 26 economists in Canada and the United States, predicted the Canadian economy would grow on average by 3.5 percent in 1997 and 3.2 percent in 1998.
Canada's economy grew by 1.5 percent in 1996.
The forecast put Canada's economy well ahead of comparable forecasts for France, Italy, Germany and Japan and slightly ahead of forecasts for the expanding U.S. and British economies.
The U.S. economy -- following its sizzling pace in the first quarter of 1997 -- was expected to grow only 3.3 percent this year and 2.2 percent in 1998, a companion U.S Reuters poll predicted.

"Canada has been a sort of sleeper for the last three or four years, but now we're seeing really hot numbers in this part of the recovery," said Jeoff Hall, a Canadian analyst and economist with Technical Data in Boston.
Hall said continued prosperity in Canada's surging export sector -- 80 percent of which is dependent upon the United States -- would be key to robust economic expansion in Canada.
"The U.S. has slowed down from its torrid pace, but the (U.S.) economy is not in an economic slowdown. That should allow the export base in Canada to thrive," Hall said.
The survey also forecast Canada's inflation rate would remain within the Bank of Canada's target range of 1 to 3 percent despite the strong growth projections.

Economists predicted on average a 1.8 percent hike in the core consumer price index (CPI) for 1997, trending up to 2 percent next year. Last year, Canada's core inflation rate, which excludes the volatile energy and food components, was 1.8 percent.
Analysts cited the Bank of Canada's apparent willingness to raise short-term interest rates as the major reason for the absence of inflation fears in the survey.
Last month, the central bank surprised markets with a 25-basis-point hike, the first time it raised interest rates in two years.
The specter of interest rate hikes in the United States and Canada was a red flag to the minority of survey participants who predicted an economic downturn in Canada.

Mark Mullins, chief economist with brokerage Midland Walwyn, suggested U.S. Federal Reserve tightening and an inevitable slowdown in the North American business cycle would force the Canadian economy into a likely recession in 1998.
"At a minimum we are going to have a good, solid growth slowdown coming into the second quarter of 1998," Mullins said.

"The status of monetary policy in the U.S. is sufficiently tight that it will bring about below-potential growth if just held where it is, but I've still got a view that we're going to get a rate hike from the Fed at the August/September meeting and one after that," Mullins said.
Fed hikes would almost certainly put enormous pressure on the Bank of Canada to follow suit, Mullins added.
Although higher Canadian interest rates should help underpin the Canadian dollar, the survey ruled out a major rebound for the currency.

Economists predicted the Canadian dollar would rally to US$0.7352 by the end of 1997 and to US$0.75 by the end of next year. The Canadian dollar currently trades at US$0.7241, down almost three percent against the U.S. dollar in the past six months.
"I get the sense that this stumble we've had recently is actually justified in terms of market confidence and information that is discounted into the currency," Mullins said.
Economic growth also will pay few dividends to unemployed Canadians.
The survey forecast Canada's annual unemployment rate would hit 9.3 percent for 1997, before dipping to 8.8 percent in 1998.
Canada's jobless rate was 9.6 percent in 1996.
"Unemployment in Canada is chronic even with the structural changes to the economy and the falling dependency on public coffers," Hall said.
((Reuters Toronto Bureau 416-941-8100))
